analogy.p: The p.d. is like the water pressure pushing, the current is the rate at which water flows past a point, and the resistance is how narrow and obstructed the pipe is. A long, narrow pipe packed with obstacles lets only a small flow through for the same pressure, just as a long thin wire has a high resistance. It breaks down because real electrons are not a fluid that can be stored, and the wire itself heats up where the water analogy shows no heating.
analogy.t: Water flowing through a pipe full of obstacles

bullets: Define resistance and state its unit, the **ohm**.
Recall and apply **V = I R**, rearranging for current or resistance.
State that current through a resistor at constant temperature is **directly proportional** to p.d.
Know that some components have a resistance that **changes** (it depends on the current or on temperature or light).
Carry out and evaluate the **required practical** on the resistance of a wire.
Handle unit prefixes: mA, kilohm and megohm.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This spec point sits at the heart of the Electricity topic. You must understand what **resistance** is, be able to use the equation **potential difference = current x resistance (V = I R)** in any arrangement, and know how resistance depends on the conductor. You must also know that for a **resistor at constant temperature** the current is directly proportional to the p.d., and that the resistance of components such as lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is **not constant**. The linked required practical investigates how the resistance of a wire depends on its length.

bullets: Resistance is the **opposition to current**: high resistance means low current for the same p.d.
Unit: **ohm**, 1 ohm = 1 V / 1 A.
Symbol on circuit diagrams for a fixed resistor: a **rectangle** in the wire.
A **variable resistor** has an arrow through the rectangle: its resistance can be changed by hand.
Even good conductors such as copper wires have a small but non-zero resistance.
Resistance is why wires and components **heat up** when current flows (link to energy transfer and power).
Insulators have extremely high resistance, so almost no current flows.
core.h: What resistance is and why it matters
core.p: **Resistance** is the opposition of a component or conductor to the flow of electric current. The larger the resistance, the smaller the current that a given potential difference can drive through it. Resistance is measured in **ohms**, written with the symbol for the ohm (spelled out as 'ohm' in these notes). One ohm is the resistance when a p.d. of 1 V drives a current of 1 A. Resistance is a property of the **component**, whereas current and p.d. describe what is happening in the circuit at that moment.

bullets: **V = I R** (p.d. in V, current in A, resistance in ohm).
Rearranged for current: **I = V / R**.
Rearranged for resistance: **R = V / I**.
Use the **formula triangle** (V on top, I and R underneath) if you need help rearranging, but also know how to rearrange algebraically.
The equation applies to the **whole circuit** or to **one component**, as long as V, I and R all refer to the same component.
Quote answers with the correct unit; a missing unit loses the final mark.
Check that the answer is sensible: a higher resistance must give a lower current.
core.p: The relationship between the three quantities is **potential difference (V) = current (I) x resistance (R)**. The potential difference is in **volts (V)**, the current is in **amperes (A)** and the resistance is in **ohms**. This equation is on the AQA equation list in a form you must recall, so memorise it. It follows from the definition of the ohm: for a fixed resistance, doubling the p.d. doubles the current. Because it links three quantities, any one can be found if the other two are known.

bullets: Step 1: **write the equation** you will use (for example V = I R).
Step 2: **convert units**: 250 mA = 0.250 A; 4.7 kilohm = 4700 ohm.
Step 3: **substitute** the numbers into the rearranged equation.
Step 4: **calculate** and give the answer to a sensible number of significant figures (usually the same as the data given).
Step 5: **write the unit** (V, A or ohm) with the answer.
Step 6: **check** the size: is the current smaller when the resistance is bigger?
Prefixes: milli (m) = 1/1000 = x 0.001; kilo (k) = x 1000; mega (M) = x 1 000 000.
core.h: Using the equation step by step
core.p: Every calculation question can be solved with the same method that earns full marks. First write down the equation, then substitute with the units converted to V, A and ohm, and finally calculate and state the unit. Writing the equation first earns the method mark even if the arithmetic goes wrong. Most errors come from forgetting to convert milliamperes to amperes or kilohms to ohms before substituting.

bullets: **I is directly proportional to V** when R is constant: I = V / R.
A graph of **V against I** is a straight line through the origin; its **gradient = V / I = R**.
On a graph of **I against V** the gradient is **1 / R**, so a steeper line means a smaller resistance.
Ohmic conductors only obey this if the **temperature stays constant**.
Doubling p.d. doubles current; halving p.d. halves current.
Typical fixed resistors keep the same resistance over a wide range of currents provided they do not overheat.
This is the rule tested in the I-V characteristic practical (next spec point).
core.h: Current and p.d. for a resistor at constant temperature
core.p: For a **fixed resistor at constant temperature**, the current through it is **directly proportional** to the potential difference across it. This means doubling the p.d. doubles the current, and the resistance V / I stays the same value every time. A conductor that behaves this way is called an **ohmic conductor**. A graph of current against p.d. for such a resistor is a straight line through the origin; the same is true for a graph of p.d. against current.

bullets: Electrons are pushed through the wire by the p.d. of the cell.
Collisions with ions **transfer energy** to the ions, which vibrate more: the wire **heats up**.
This is the **heating effect of a current**, and it is why electrical resistance causes energy to be wasted as thermal energy.
More ions in the path of the electrons (a **longer** wire) means more collisions, so greater resistance.
A **thicker** wire gives the electrons more room to move, so fewer collisions per electron and a lower resistance.
Raising the **temperature** makes ions vibrate more, so the electrons collide more often, raising the resistance of a metal.
Use the phrase **'more frequent collisions between electrons and ions'** in explanations.
core.h: Why a conductor has resistance: electrons and ions
core.p: In a metal wire the current is a flow of **free (delocalised) electrons** drifting through a lattice of positive **ions**. As the electrons move they **collide with the ions**, and each collision transfers some energy from the electrons to the ions. This opposition to the flow is resistance, and the energy transferred makes the ions vibrate more, which is why the wire gets hot. A greater number of collisions per second means a higher resistance.

bullets: **Longer wire = greater resistance** (directly proportional at constant temperature).
**Thicker wire (larger cross-sectional area) = smaller resistance**.
**Material**: copper has low resistance; nichrome and constantan have higher resistance, so they are used for heating elements and resistance wire.
**Temperature**: for a metal wire, higher temperature gives higher resistance.
Doubling the length **and** doubling the area leaves the resistance unchanged.
Cables carrying large currents are thick copper to keep the resistance low and prevent overheating.
Think of resistance as **how crowded the path is**: longer and narrower means harder to push charge through.
core.h: Factors affecting the resistance of a wire
core.p: The resistance of a wire depends on its **length**, its **cross-sectional area**, the **material** it is made from and its **temperature**. For a given material at constant temperature, resistance is directly proportional to length, so doubling the length doubles the resistance, because the electrons pass twice as many ions. Resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area, so doubling the area halves the resistance. These ideas explain why power cables are thick and why heating elements are thin, long wires of high-resistance alloys.

bullets: **Filament lamp**: as current rises the filament gets hotter and **resistance increases**; I-V graph curves.
**Diode**: allows current in **one direction only**; very high resistance in the reverse direction.
**Thermistor** (NTC): resistance **decreases** as temperature rises.
**LDR**: resistance **decreases** as light intensity increases.
For these components current is **not** proportional to p.d.; they are **non-ohmic**.
To find the resistance at a point, read V and I at that point and calculate R = V / I (do not use the gradient of a curve at the point).
These components are covered in detail in the next spec points.
core.h: Components whose resistance is not constant
core.p: The straight-line relationship only holds for fixed resistors at constant temperature. Some components have a resistance that **changes** as the current or the conditions change. In a **filament lamp**, the current heats the filament so its resistance increases with temperature. A **diode** has a very high resistance in one direction. A **thermistor** has a resistance that depends on temperature and a **light-dependent resistor (LDR)** has a resistance that depends on light intensity. For these components the resistance at any moment is still found from R = V / I using the values at that point.

bullets: Set up a series circuit: **cell (or low-voltage supply), ammeter, test wire** fixed along a metre ruler.
Connect the **voltmeter in parallel** with the section of test wire between the two crocodile clips.
Attach one clip at 0.100 m and the other at 0.200 m so the length between them is **0.100 m**; close the switch.
Record the **p.d. and current**, then open the switch immediately to stop the wire heating.
Repeat for lengths 0.200 m, 0.300 m ... up to about 1.000 m by moving one clip.
Calculate **R = V / I** for each length and plot **resistance against length**.
Repeat each length and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability.
core.h: Required practical: the resistance of a wire (method)
core.p: This required practical investigates how the **resistance of a wire depends on its length**. You measure the current through a length of wire and the p.d. across it, then calculate the resistance for each length using R = V / I. The independent variable is the length of wire in the circuit, the dependent variable is the resistance, and the control variables are the wire material, its diameter and the temperature.

bullets: Control variables: **same wire material, same diameter, same temperature**.
**Switch off between readings**, otherwise the wire heats and its resistance rises (a systematic error).
Use a **low p.d.** (for example 2 V to 4 V) so the heating is small.
Hazards: a hot wire can cause **burns**, so allow it to cool and do not touch it during the experiment.
**Contact resistance** at the crocodile clips adds a small resistance to every reading, giving a graph that does not pass through the origin.
Measure the length from the **inside edges** of the clips and read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax.
Check the meters for **zero error** before starting; use a **repeat and mean** to find anomalies.
core.h: Practical: variables, safety and sources of error
core.p: A good answer to a practical question names the variables exactly and explains how each is controlled. The independent variable is **length**, the dependent variable is **resistance (calculated from V and I)** and the **controlled variables** include the wire (same material and thickness), the supply p.d. and the temperature. The main problem is that the wire heats up as current flows, which changes the resistance, so the current must be kept low and switched off between readings.

bullets: Plot **independent variable (length) on the x-axis**, dependent (resistance) on the y-axis.
Draw a **line of best fit** with a ruler; ignore anomalies but state them.
**Gradient = change in R / change in l** = resistance per metre (units ohm per metre).
If you double the length and the resistance doubles, **R is proportional to l**.
Use the line to **predict the resistance** of a length not tested (interpolation).
A **curve** upward suggests heating of the wire during the measurement.
Compare gradients of thick and thin wire: the thinner wire has the **steeper** line.
core.h: Analysing the data and the graph
core.p: A graph of resistance (y-axis) against length (x-axis) should be a **straight line through the origin**, showing that resistance is directly proportional to length. The gradient of this line is the **resistance per metre** of the wire, which is a property of the wire material and thickness. If the line has a positive intercept on the resistance axis, a likely reason is the contact resistance of the clips and leads; if the points curve upward, the wire may have been heating.

bullets: Convert **mA to A** by dividing by 1000 before using V = I R.
Convert **kilohm to ohm** by multiplying by 1000.
Do not use the cell's p.d. as the p.d. across a component unless they are the same; in a series circuit with other components the p.d. is shared.
When asked for **current**, divide V by R; when asked for **resistance**, divide V by I.
If R increases and V stays the same, **I decreases**.
In '**explain**' questions on temperature, mention **ions vibrating more** and **more frequent collisions**.
Give the unit **ohm** (not 'ohms' as a symbol only) and check the order of magnitude.
core.h: Common traps and checks for calculations
core.p: Examiners set resistance questions in several ways, and the same traps appear again and again. Always convert milliamperes, check that the p.d. you use is the one across the component, and be careful when rearranging. Also look at the command word: 'calculate' needs working and a unit, while 'explain' needs a reason that links collisions and temperature.

bullets: **Series circuits**: total resistance is the sum of the resistances (R total = R1 + R2).
**Parallel circuits**: adding a branch lowers the total resistance.
**Power**: P = I squared x R uses the same resistance; resistance explains why wires heat up.
**National Grid**: step-up transformers reduce the current so less energy is wasted as heat in the cables.
**Charge**: Q = I t links current to the charge flowing; p.d. relates to energy per unit charge.
**Sensors**: thermistors and LDRs are used in switching circuits because their resistance changes.
**Higher tier extension**: a graph of V against I for any component can be used to find R at a point, and the gradient of a straight line gives R.
core.p: Resistance connects directly to the rest of Electricity. The ideas of series and parallel circuits are built on V = I R, the power equations use the same quantities, and the energy wasted in a resistor explains why long, thin cables are inefficient. It also appears in mains electricity and in the National Grid, where high voltage transmission reduces the current and so the energy wasted as heat.

exam: **Calculate** (2 marks): equation and substitution for 1 mark, correct answer with unit for the second. Always show working.
**State** that the current is directly proportional to p.d. for a resistor at constant temperature (1 mark).
**Explain** why a wire gets hot (2 to 3 marks): electrons collide with ions, transferring energy so the ions vibrate more and the wire's thermal energy increases.
**Explain** why the resistance of a metal increases with temperature (2 marks): ions vibrate more, more frequent collisions with electrons.

**Describe** the practical (up to 6 marks): circuit with ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel, vary the length, calculate R = V / I, repeat and plot, control variables, switch off to avoid heating.
**Evaluate** a graph: line of best fit through the origin shows R is proportional to l; a positive intercept suggests contact resistance.
Use the phrase '**directly proportional**' for a straight line through the origin; 'proportional' alone may not score.
For 4 mark questions plan: variable, apparatus, measurements, calculation, a control.
Read the question for the **component** to which V and I belong before substituting.
State **units** every time; check significant figures against the data.
On a V-I graph of a resistor, the gradient equals **R**; on an I-V graph, the gradient equals **1 / R**.

mistakes.r: Convert to amperes first, otherwise the answer is a thousand times too large.
mistakes.w: Using V = I R without converting 250 mA to 0.25 A.

mistakes.r: Resistance is the opposition to current; current is the rate of flow of charge.
mistakes.w: Resistance is the same as current.

mistakes.r: The voltmeter goes in parallel; the ammeter goes in series.
mistakes.w: The voltmeter goes in series with the component.

mistakes.r: Electrons are not used up; they transfer energy to the ions and the current is the same all around a series loop.
mistakes.w: Electrons are used up by the resistor.

mistakes.r: A longer wire has greater resistance because electrons collide with more ions.
mistakes.w: A longer wire has less resistance because the electrons have farther to go.

mistakes.r: Resistance of a metal wire increases with temperature because ions vibrate more and collide with electrons more frequently.
mistakes.w: Resistance of a wire does not change when it heats up.

mistakes.r: The wire heats up, so the resistance changes; switch off between readings to keep the temperature constant.
mistakes.w: Leaving the circuit switched on between readings is fine.

mistakes.r: Always write the unit, for example 12 ohm.
mistakes.w: Writing the answer 12 with no unit.

summary: You must understand resistance as the opposition to current, use V = I R in any arrangement with correct units, know that current is directly proportional to p.d. for a resistor at constant temperature, and carry out the wire-length required practical. It matters because every circuit calculation in Paper 1 depends on it.

terms.d: The opposition of a component to the flow of current; measured in ohms.
The unit of resistance; 1 ohm is the resistance when a p.d. of 1 volt drives a current of 1 ampere.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit; measured in volts.
The rate of flow of electrical charge; measured in amperes.
A conductor for which the current is directly proportional to the p.d. at constant temperature.
Two quantities whose ratio is constant; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed, used to change the current in a circuit.
A lamp in which the resistance increases as the filament gets hotter.
Measures p.d. across a component; connected in parallel.
The area of the cut face of a wire; thicker wire has a larger area and a lower resistance.
Extra resistance at connections such as crocodile clips, which causes a positive intercept.
A variable kept the same so that only the independent variable affects the result.

worked.q: A resistor has a p.d. of 12 V across it and a current of 0.40 A through it. Calculate its resistance. (2 marks)
steps: Write the equation: R = V / I.

worked.q: A student measures a current of 25 mA through a 2.4 kilohm resistor. Calculate the potential difference across it. (3 marks)

worked.ans: A full-mark answer includes the circuit (ammeter series, voltmeter parallel), the changing length, R = V / I, the control of temperature and wire, repeats and the graph.
worked.q: Describe how you would investigate the relationship between the length of a wire and its resistance. (6 marks)
steps: Set up a series circuit with a cell, ammeter, switch and the test wire stretched along a metre ruler.
Connect a voltmeter in parallel across the section of wire between two crocodile clips.
Set the clips 0.100 m apart, close the switch, and record the p.d. and current; open the switch straight away so the wire does not heat.
Calculate the resistance using R = V / I.
Repeat for lengths up to 1.000 m, using the same wire, and repeat each length to calculate a mean.
Plot resistance against length; a straight line through the origin shows resistance is directly proportional to length.
